title: WA Cares and the estate tax
teaches: Washington's payroll premium for long-term care and what it pays, and the state estate tax, which starts at $3 million and isn't shared between spouses

parts.title: Two state programmes at the end of life

blocks.text: Two Washington rules touch many households that work in the state and save well, and both are easy to miss: a payroll premium for long-term care that comes off every paycheque, and an estate tax that starts at one fifth of the federal threshold.

Since July 2023, employees in Washington pay 0.58 percent of their wages, with no upper limit, into WA Cares, a state fund for long-term care.[^opt-out] Someone earning $150,000 pays $870 a year. From July 2026 the fund pays benefits: up to $36,500 over a lifetime, raised with inflation, for someone who needs help with at least three daily activities such as bathing, dressing or eating. It pays for care at home, in a facility, or to a family member trained as a carer.

To qualify, a person must have paid for ten years, with no gap of five or more years in a row, or for three of the last six years. A year counts if they worked at least 500 hours in it. Those born before 1968 earn a tenth of the benefit for each year they paid. The early retiree is the case the rules weren't drawn for: someone who stops work at 50 at the end of 2026 has paid for three and a half years, from mid-2023. Looking back six years, they still have three paid years in the window until about the end of 2029, and then the cover lapses.[^vesting]

The benefit is modest beside the costs in the long-term care lesson: $36,500 pays for about three months in a private room in a Washington nursing home. It is best thought of as a first layer: it pays for help at home early on, before savings, insurance or Medicaid take over. A 2024 law lets people who leave Washington, after at least three years of paying, keep their eligibility by choosing to stay in the programme and paying premiums themselves, under rules that start in 2026.[^portable]

Each estate tax has an **exclusion**, the amount an estate can hold before any tax is due. The federal exclusion is $15 million per person in 2026, and whatever one spouse doesn't use can be added to the other's, so a couple has $30 million. Washington's is $3 million per person in 2026, raised with inflation in later years, and a spouse's unused part can't be added to the other's. Above the exclusion, for deaths from July 2026, Washington takes 10 percent of the first $1 million, then 14, 15 and 16 percent on the next three, rising by smaller steps to 20 percent above $9 million.
Those rates have just changed back. For deaths from July 2025 to June 2026 the top rate was 35 percent; a law signed in March 2026 returned it to 20 percent for deaths from July 2026.[^rates]

Everything counts: the house, retirement accounts at full value with no allowance for the income tax heirs will pay on them, life insurance the person owned, and their share of anything owned jointly, usually half of what a couple owns together. A Seattle couple with a paid-off house and well-funded 401(k)s can be worth more than $3 million each without thinking of themselves as rich.

blocks.caption: Washington estate tax on a couple's estate after both deaths, leaving everything to the survivor or placing one exclusion in a trust at the first death, for deaths from July 2026, without growth.
blocks.task: Guess, then compare the two plans

blocks.text: The simplest will, leaving everything to the spouse and then to the children, wastes one exclusion. Nothing is taxed at the first death, because gifts to a spouse are exempt, but the survivor's estate then holds everything and has only one $3 million exclusion. For a $6 million couple, the second estate is taxed on $3 million: 10, 14 and 15 percent on the three slices, $390,000 that the children lose.

The usual fix is a trust created at the first death, holding up to $3 million for the survivor's benefit but outside their estate. The survivor can have its income and, within limits, its principal; at the second death it passes to the heirs untaxed. A will can also leave the choice open: the survivor can **disclaim**, formally refuse, part of the inheritance within nine months of the death, and the will sends what they refuse into such a trust, once the numbers are known.

Three other routes reduce the estate itself. Washington has no gift tax, so gifts during life leave the estate, and Washington doesn't add them back at death. Gifts up to $19,000 a year per recipient need no federal paperwork; larger ones use up part of the $15 million federal exclusion, which few households come near. Gifts to charity at death are deducted in full. And retirement accounts left to charity, which pays no income tax on them, are the cheapest assets to give, as the taxable branch's lesson on giving and heirs shows.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: WA Cares takes 0.58 percent of wages and pays up to $36,500 of long-term care from July 2026, with eligibility after ten years or three of the last six.
An early retiree can lose WA Cares eligibility a few years after stopping work if they haven't paid for ten.
Washington's estate tax starts at $3 million a person and isn't portable between spouses; rates for deaths from July 2026 run from 10 to 20 percent.
Leaving everything to the survivor wastes an exclusion; a trust at the first death keeps both.
The house and retirement accounts count in full, so many ordinary savers cross $3 million.

blocks.caption: Five questions on WA Cares and the estate tax
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How much does WA Cares pay at most over a lifetime, starting July 2026?
items.why: It is a lifetime total, enough for a first layer of care rather than all of it.

items.ask: Someone paid into WA Cares for four years and stopped work at 50. What happens to their eligibility?
choices: It lasts only while three of the last six years are paid
They get 40 percent of the benefit for life
items.why: Permanent eligibility needs ten years; the partial benefit by years paid is for people born before 1968.

items.ask: A widower dies in 2027 with a $5 million estate. Can his executor use his late wife's unused Washington exclusion?
choices: Yes, the estate has $6 million exempt
items.why: Unlike the federal exclusion, Washington's can't pass from one spouse to the other.

items.ask: What does a trust at the first death achieve for a Washington couple?
choices: It uses the first spouse's exclusion
It avoids federal income tax on IRAs
It removes the house from property tax
items.why: Up to $3 million goes into the trust, outside the survivor's estate, so both exclusions are used.

items.ask: Which assets count towards a Washington estate?
choices: The house, retirement accounts and owned life insurance, all in full
Only assets above the federal threshold
items.why: The estate includes everything owned at death, with retirement accounts at full value.

summary: **WA Cares is a payroll premium for care.** 0.58 percent of wages, for up to $36,500 of help from July 2026.
**Eligibility needs ten years or recent work.** An early retiree who stops sooner can lose it within a few years.
**Washington's estate tax starts at $3 million.** A fifth of the federal threshold, at 10 to 20 percent from July 2026.
**It isn't portable between spouses.** Leaving everything to the survivor wastes one exclusion.
**A trust at the first death keeps both.** A disclaimer can leave the choice to the survivor.
**Everything counts in full.** House, retirement accounts and owned life insurance all go in.

vesting.title: The three ways to qualify
vesting.text: The ten years need at least 500 hours of work in each. The three-of-six test is checked when care is needed. People born before 1968 who pay for at least one year earn 10 percent of the benefit for each year paid, without needing ten.

portable.title: Leaving the state
portable.text: As first passed, WA Cares paid only to people living in Washington. The 2024 change lets someone who moves away elect to continue paying premiums after at least three years of contributions, and to draw benefits elsewhere once qualified.

rates.title: Two schedules in one year
rates.text: The 2025 law raised the exclusion from $2.193 million to $3 million and the top rate from 20 to 35 percent. The 2026 law kept the higher exclusion and restored rates of 10 to 20 percent. An estate is taxed on the schedule in force on the date of death.

opt-out.title: The 2021 opt-out rush
opt-out.text: Workers who bought private long-term care insurance before November 2021 could apply for a permanent exemption from WA Cares.nearly half a million people did, flooding insurers until most stopped selling policies in the state. Narrower exemptions remain for workers who live outside Washington, military spouses and veterans with service-connected disabilities.
